hints: Look at the two changes separately, concentration affects how often particles meet, while temperature affects how much energy they have.
Halving both concentrations will tend to lower collision frequency, but raising temperature from 298 K to 348 K gives all particles more kinetic energy.
Ask yourself which effect is guaranteed by temperature alone, regardless of how the concentration change and temperature change compete for rate.
walkthrough:
**Separate the two changes**

Think like a teacher with two dials. Dial 1 is concentration halved, dial 2 is temperature raised.

Reaction:
$$X(aq) + Y(aq) \rightarrow XY(aq)$$

**Recall what temperature definitely does**

Temperature is a measure of average kinetic energy. Higher T means faster moving particles and more energy per particle.

Rule:
$$\text{average kinetic energy} \propto T \text{ (in Kelvin)}$$

**Check concentration versus temperature on collisions**

Lower concentration means fewer particles per volume, so fewer collisions. Higher temperature means more frequent and more energetic collisions.

So the two changes push collision frequency in opposite directions. We cannot be sure of the net result.

**Decide what is definitely true**

The only guaranteed effect is from temperature on energy. From 298 K to 348 K, average kinetic energy must increase, and a larger proportion of collisions will have energy $\ge E_a$.

options.A: Incorrect. The proportion of successful collisions depends on activation energy and temperature, not concentration. Since temperature increases, a larger proportion, not a smaller proportion, will have energy greater than or equal to Ea.
options.B: Correct. Average kinetic energy is directly proportional to absolute temperature. Increasing T from 298 K to 348 K definitely increases the average kinetic energy of X and Y particles.
options.C: Incorrect. Halving concentrations tends to decrease rate, while increasing temperature tends to increase rate. The net effect could be an increase, decrease or no change, so we cannot definitely say it is unaffected.
options.D: Incorrect. Halving both concentrations alone would reduce collision frequency to about one quarter, not one half, but the temperature rise also increases collision frequency. The combined result is uncertain, so it will not definitely halve.
